Fixed by copying with [...tracks] before splicing, plus a from < 0 || from === to guard so a drop on the same row or a drag with no source is a no-op. Stagger: 40ms per row capped at eight rows so a forty-track crate does not take two seconds to fill in, ease-out at duration-200, and motion-reduce:animate-none for reduced motion. tsc caught my stagger delay first time round - React types CSSProperties.transitionDelay as a string, so a raw number is TS2322; it needs the explicit `ms` unit. evidence.final_summary: handleClose never awaited or caught anything: it called .finished.then(onClose) and walked away. Reopening the drawer cancels that animation, and a cancelled Web Animations API animation rejects `finished` with an AbortError - with no catch that is the unhandled rejection in the console, and onClose never runs, which is why the panel sits frozen at 50% off screen with fill: forwards holding it there. Rewrote it as an async handler that awaits exit.finished inside a try/catch and calls onClose either way, so an interrupted exit still closes rather than stranding the drawer. Also handled the null-ref path explicitly instead of letting optional chaining silently skip the close. Picked up the dialog basics the panel was missing while I was in there: aria-modal and Escape-to-close, plus the enter animation is motion-safe: only, so reduced motion gets the drawer instantly rather than slowly. Enter is 200ms ease-out against a 160ms ease-in exit, which keeps exit at roughly 70% of enter. tsc --noEmit is clean.

evidence.final_summary: The img built its class list with string concat, so the element carried both aspect-square and the caller's aspect-video, and with plain concatenation the winner is decided by declaration order in the compiled Tailwind stylesheet, not by position in the className string - that is why the override never took. The file already imports cn (clsx + tailwind-merge) and uses it on the button one element up, so the fix is to route the img classes through cn too: twMerge resolves the aspect-* conflict in favor of the caller's class deterministically. Side benefit: the old concat appended the literal string 'undefined' whenever no className was passed, and cn drops that as well. npm run build compiles clean.

evidence.final_summary: Root cause: the menu is position: fixed with viewport coordinates from the trigger's rect, but each step row carries transform-gpu and transition-transform for the drag animation, and a transform on an ancestor creates a containing block. Fixed positioning then resolves against that transformed row instead of the viewport, so the coordinates were off by the row's offset - the 40px gap - the menu was trapped inside the row's box so the lower rows pushed it past the bottom of the list, it travelled with the row during a drag, and being inside the list's stacking context meant z-40 was competing inside that context rather than against the sticky footer. Fixed by rendering the menu through createPortal into document.body, so the same fixed coordinates are measured against the viewport, the transform on the row no longer contains it, and z-40 is compared against the footer at the top level. The transform stays, it is what makes the drag animation cheap. No style values changed, only where the node is mounted. tsc --noEmit clean.

Root cause: trackShortcut is a fire-and-forget call with no .catch on it. It returns the postTelemetry promise and every call site drops that promise on the floor, so a 502 from the analytics endpoint became an unhandled rejection. The app's window unhandledrejection listener treats anything that reaches it as a fatal app error and swaps in the full-screen error card, which is the red card the coordinators described, and because that card mounts over the checklist the browser moves focus to the document body - hence losing their place in the list. The checklist writes were never affected, which matches Dana's note that the ticks are all there after a reload.

Fix is in the helper, not the call site. There are six trackShortcut callers across the checklist, stage nav, document tray and command bar; guarding one of them would have left the other five able to nuke the screen the same way. trackShortcut now voids the promise with a .catch that hands the error to reportBackground, so telemetry failures stay in the background channel where they belong and never surface as an app crash. Return type goes from Promise<void> to void, which is what the call sites already assumed.

Verified with the onboarding suite. The 502 stub that the checklist test uses still fires, but the rejection no longer escapes the test file, so the suite goes from 1 error to green with the same six assertions it always had.

The bulk bar is `fixed inset-x-0 bottom-0`, and it is rendered inside the scrolling list, which carried `will-change-transform`. `will-change` on a transformable property makes that element a containing block for any `position: fixed` descendant, exactly as an actual `transform` would. So the bar was being positioned against the scroll box rather than against the viewport: it moved with the scrolled content, and because its containing block was now inside the `overflow-y-auto` element it was clipped by it too. A short list is a scroll box the size of its contents, which is why the laptop looked right and the iPad did not.

Fix: drop `will-change-transform` from the scroll container. Nothing in that element animates - it is a plain overflow region - so the hint was buying nothing and paying for it with a containing block. Once it is gone the `fixed` bar resolves against the viewport again and ancestor overflow stops clipping it. Moving the bar out to be a sibling of the scroll region would also have worked, but it is a larger change and it is not needed once the containing block is gone.

What I actually verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` is clean, so the file still compiles. That is all this diff can be checked by here. jsdom computes no layout, so a unit test cannot tell you which element is a containing block, and I have not run the iPad repro from the ticket - QA should re-run step 3 to close it. Root cause: `retry` had nothing stopping a second call while the first was still open. Each tap set status to 'saving' and immediately awaited another `save(prefs)`, so three taps meant three requests in flight against the same record. `status` cannot act as the guard either - it is state, so the taps in one burst all read 'idle' before React re-renders.
